title: How a Request Travels
subtitle: Follow one page load from the Enter key to the last byte, and see which hops eat the time.
learn: What a DNS lookup does and when it is skipped
Why TCP and TLS setup cost round trips before any data moves
The path browser → load balancer → app server → database and back
Why distance and a slow dependency can dominate page load time

steps.title: You press Enter
steps.body: You type shop.example and press Enter. Half a second later, a page appears. That short wait is really a chain of small conversations between machines. Each one must finish before the next can start. This lesson follows the chain in order and times every link.
steps.idea: A page load is a chain of waits. The total time is their sum.
steps.caption: The browser knows a name, but not yet an address.

steps.title: Find the address
steps.body: The animation shows the browser asking a DNS resolver and getting an IP address back. Computers find each other by IP address (like a phone number), not by name. DNS, the Domain Name System, is the phone book that turns shop.example into 203.0.113.7. If the answer was saved recently (cached), the lookup is almost free. The saved answer lives for a time set by its TTL (time to live). A first lookup may ask several servers and take tens of milliseconds. Here we use 20 ms.
steps.idea: DNS turns a name into an IP address. A cached answer makes this step nearly free.
steps.caption: The resolver replies with an IP address (20 ms).

steps.title: Open a secure connection
steps.body: Next the browser opens a secure connection to the load balancer, the front door of the site. First comes TCP, a handshake that makes sure both sides are ready (1 round trip). Then comes TLS, which sets up encryption (1 more round trip with TLS 1.3). A round trip, or RTT, is a message going out and its reply coming back. We assume 50 ms per round trip, so setup costs about 100 ms before any page data moves. The DNS answer is now cached, so later requests skip that lookup.
steps.idea: Every handshake costs a full round trip, so distance multiplies directly into delay.
steps.caption: Four handshake messages make 2 round trips: about 100 ms.

steps.title: Send the request
steps.body: Now the browser sends GET /, which means 'give me the home page', along with headers and cookies. The load balancer receives it and passes it to one healthy app server. Think of it as a receptionist who sends each visitor to a free desk. This lets any single server fail or be replaced without users noticing. The request takes about 25 ms to travel one way, so the clock reads 145 ms.
steps.idea: The load balancer hides how many servers exist and which one answers.
steps.caption: The request travels 25 ms and is forwarded to an app server.

steps.title: Fetch the data
steps.body: The app server needs data to build the page: the product list, the cart, the prices. So it sends a query to the database. A query that uses an index (like a book's index, it lets the database jump straight to the rows) comes back in about 4 ms. The server then builds the HTML from those rows. All server work here totals 40 ms, bringing the clock to 185 ms.
steps.idea: Server time is the app's own work plus every dependency it waits on.
steps.caption: The app asks the database and gets rows back.

steps.title: Bytes come back
steps.body: The finished HTML travels back through the load balancer to the browser. The first byte arrives at 210 ms: 185 ms plus 25 ms of travel. That moment is called TTFB (time to first byte), a common speed measure. The browser can start reading right away. The last of the HTML finishes downloading 25 ms later, at 235 ms.
steps.idea: TTFB includes DNS, connect, request and server time, but not the full download.
steps.caption: HTML flows back: first byte at 210 ms, finished at 235 ms.

steps.title: More files
steps.body: The HTML lists more files: CSS (styling), JavaScript (behavior), fonts and images. The browser fetches them from a CDN (content delivery network), servers placed near users that keep copies of static files. A separate CDN hostname needs its own lookup and handshake, but the edge is close, so that stays cheap. Several files download in parallel and together add about 75 ms, so the page is ready at 310 ms. On a repeat visit most of these come from the browser's own cache.
steps.idea: Serving static files from a nearby edge removes distance from most of the bytes.
steps.caption: Static files arrive from a nearby CDN edge (+75 ms).

steps.title: A slow query
steps.body: What if the query has no index and must read every row (a full scan)? Suppose it takes 900 ms instead of 4 ms. Server time grows from 40 ms to 900 ms and the total becomes 1,170 ms. Nothing else changed. The critical path is the chain of steps that must happen one after another. One slow step on it sets the speed of the whole page. That is why you measure each hop instead of guessing.
steps.idea: The slowest hop on the critical path usually dominates the total, so fix that one first.
steps.caption: One slow query now dominates the whole page load.

steps.title: A faraway user
steps.body: Go back to the healthy 40 ms query, but put the user on another continent, 150 ms away by round trip. Setup is 2 round trips, so 2 × 150 = 300 ms. The request and its reply add another 150 ms. In total: DNS 20 + setup 300 + request and reply 150 + server 40 = 510 ms to the first byte. A nearby user gets it at about 210 ms. Faster code cannot beat the speed of light. Moving servers or caches closer to users can.
steps.idea: Latency from distance is paid per round trip, so fewer round trips and closer servers both help.
steps.caption: Each round trip now costs 150 ms; first byte at about 510 ms.

steps.title: Where the time went
steps.body: A page load is DNS, connect, request, server work, response, then assets, in that order. Caching cuts DNS and asset time. Reusing connections cuts handshakes. Indexes cut server time. CDNs and nearby servers cut distance. To speed up a page, first find which hop is slow. This lesson times only the network and server hops. Parsing, drawing the page and running JavaScript add more time after the last byte.
steps.idea: Measure each hop, then fix the biggest one.
steps.caption: Every hop added to the total: 310 ms for a nearby user.

quiz.q: A page's DNS lookup takes 0 ms on a repeat visit. What is the most likely reason?
options: DNS is skipped for HTTPS sites
The answer was cached and its TTL had not expired
The load balancer stores IP addresses
quiz.why: Resolvers, the OS, and browsers cache DNS answers until their TTL expires, so repeat lookups are near-instant.

quiz.q: The server is 80 ms away (round trip). Roughly how long do a fresh TCP + TLS 1.3 handshake take before the request can be sent?
quiz.why: TCP needs one round trip and TLS 1.3 needs one more, so about two round trips: 2 × 80 ms.

quiz.q: TTFB jumps from 200 ms to 1.2 s after a deploy, but DNS and connect times are unchanged. Where should you look first?
options: Server-side work such as a slow database query
quiz.why: If DNS and connection setup are unchanged, the added time is inside the server's handling, typically a slow dependency like a query.

cheatsheet.def: Round-trip time: how long a message takes to reach a server and come back. Handshakes cost whole RTTs.

Time to first byte: from the start of the navigation until the first response byte arrives, so it includes redirects, DNS, TCP/TLS setup, request travel and server time. Some tools (e.g. the DevTools 'waiting' bar) count only from request-sent.
One round trip to agree on keys before encrypted data can flow (TLS 1.2 needed two). Optional 0-RTT resumption can send data in the first flight, but has replay risks and is used sparingly.
The longest chain of dependent steps. Its total length is the fastest the request can finish, so speeding up anything off this chain does not help.
